Field Journal
LatestTopicsAbout

Design / Field notes

Make space for the work that matters.

A practical guide to building calmer routines and clearer digital spaces.

By Alex Rivera8 minute readSeptember 18, 2026

Good interfaces do not need to shout. They help people find a useful next step without hiding the context around it.

Begin with a clear hierarchy

Choose one main idea for the page. Give headings, body copy, and supporting labels distinct roles, and keep line lengths comfortable as the viewport changes.

Then test the content with a longer heading, a small screen, and text enlargement. A layout should remain readable when real content is less predictable than the sample.

“Clarity is not less information; it is information with a useful shape.”

Design for more than the default screen

Use responsive constraints, visible keyboard focus, and a print stylesheet when readers may need a paper copy. Avoid hiding essential meaning in a decorative image.

About the author

Alex writes about thoughtful product design and practical workflows.

required_features: Readable line length and vertical rhythm
stretch_features: Add a second theme using custom properties.
Test at 320 CSS pixels, 768 CSS pixels, and a wide desktop viewport.
Document browser support assumptions and any fallback for optional CSS features.

tests.name: Required CSS checks
criteria: All listed required features are present and behave as described.
Inspect the stylesheet for invalid declarations and unintended overrides.
Check keyboard focus, responsive reflow, and reduced-motion handling where relevant.

tests.name: Responsive behavior
criteria: No unintended horizontal overflow at narrow widths.
Layout remains coherent when text is longer than sample content.

tests.name: Maintainability
criteria: Reusable tokens and component classes are used intentionally.
Known feature support limits and design choices are documented.

review_method: Human-reviewed visual and accessibility evaluation supported by the listed checks; CSS string checks alone cannot prove rendered behavior.
